newsitem.title: USA: Gore, Kemp battle over taxes, economy.
newsitem.headline: Gore, Kemp battle over taxes, economy.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore and Republican challenger Jack Kemp haggled over taxes, the economy and foreign policy Wednesday in a cerebral televised debate marked by a civil, scholarly tone.

Kemp, seeking to give Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole a boost in his uphill battle against President Clinton, got in the first swing by saying he had only two disagreements with Clinton and Gore -- their domestic policy and their foreign policy.

He said Americans are "overtaxed, over-regulated," and that Clinton-Gore proposals for targeted tax cuts are an overbearing intrusion into American lives. "That's not America, that's social engineering," he said.
Kemp called Clinton's foreign policy "ambiguous, confusing," and sending the wrong signals. "We have learned over the years that weakness is provocative," he said.
Gore, looking to say nothing that would hurt Clinton's large lead in the public opinion polls ahead of the Nov. 5 election, attacked Dole's proposal for a 15 percent across-the-board tax cut.

He called it "a risky, $550 billion tax scheme" that would raise taxes on 9 million hard-working families, "blow a hole in the deficit," and "knock the economy off track" by leading to higher interest rates.
"We stopped that plan before. We will stop it again. We want a positive plan for growth and more jobs," Gore said.
The contest was seen as a possible preview of the presidential race in the year 2000 when both Kemp and Gore could be carrying the banner for their parties.

The debate at Mehaffey Centre, moderated by Jim Lehrer of the Public Broadcasting System (PBS), had a civil tone from the beginning when Lehrer asked Kemp why Dole had been unwilling to draw personal and ethical differences with Clinton.
"Bob Dole and myself do not see Bill Clinton and Al Gore as our enemies. We see them as our opponents," he said. "In my opinion it is beneath Bob Dole to go after anyone personally."

Gore, delighted by the response, told Kemp that if he would not use any football stories from his days as as pro football quarterback, he would not get into the nitty-gritty of environmental policy. "I won't tell any of my warm, humorous stories about chlorofluorocarbon abatement," Gore said, drawing a laugh from the audience.
The debate had a scholarly, brainy tone that was relatively devoid of the type of one-line zingers Dole and Clinton hurled at each other at their first debate Sunday night in Hartford, Conn.
Kemp said if elected he and Dole would bring to bear a "simpler, flatter" tax code and a less intrusive government that would give people more control over their finances and their lives.
After Gore explained the Clinton plan for a tax credit for use for education, Kemp was dismissive.
"You only get a tax cut in the Clinton administraton if you do exactly what Al Gore and Bill Clinton want you to do. That is not America," he said.
He said the government should aim to double the size of the American economy in the next 15 years. "Under their policies it will take 30 to 40 years. That's not acceptable," he said.
Gore tweaked Kemp for having changed his position from supporting affirmative action policies for minorities in order to agree with Dole's position that these policies should be ended.
"With all due respect I do not believe that Abraham Lincoln would have adopted Bob Dole's position to end all affirmative action," Gore said. Lincoln is considered the father of the Republican Party.
